# International Morse code — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/morse-code.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/morse-code.ttl`](../decks/morse-code.ttl) · **Cards:** 51 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

The International Morse code of Recommendation ITU-R M.1677-1 (the 26 letters A–Z and É, the digits 0–9 and 13 of its 14 punctuation marks and signs; × is sent as X), plus the distress signal SOS from the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea: 51 cards in all. Front: the character; back: its code, written with · for a dot and − for a dash; studied in both directions. Å, Ä and Ö are not in the current ITU recommendation and are left out. The codes come from Wikidata and the US edition of the International Code of Signals (Pub. 102), checked against the ITU recommendation and Wikipedia.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its codes come from Wikidata (CC0) and from two works of the US Government that are not protected by copyright: Pub. 102, the US edition of the International Code of Signals ("No copyright claimed under Title 17 U.S.C."), and the regulation 33 CFR 87.01. The back notes rest on these content sources as well: × and the dash share the codes of X and the hyphen (Wikidata), K is the invitation to transmit and the signal of + is the ending signal AR (Pub. 102), and SOS is the distress signal of the collision regulations, sent as one group (Pub. 102 and 33 CFR 87.01). The selection of the letters, figures and punctuation marks follows the list in Recommendation ITU-R M.1677-1, Annex 1, Part I, 1.1: the deck takes every written character the recommendation defines (except ×, which shares the signal of X). Taking all the characters a standard defines is a complete, non-creative enumeration with no originality of selection, and which characters a standard defines is a fact; neither Wikidata nor Pub. 102 identifies this set on its own. Adding SOS and leaving out × and the procedural signals is the compiler's own choice. The notation, the front notes (English and Swedish names of the marks, from Wikidata labels or common Swedish words checked on Swedish Wikipedia) and the back notes are the compiler's own wording. Recommendation ITU-R M.1677-1 (© ITU, all rights reserved) and the English and Swedish Wikipedia articles (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used for verification only: they confirmed the codes and notes that the cards have from the content sources and the deck's statements of scope (the code of a character is a fact, not protected by copyright), and no text, table, layout or note was copied from them.

## Method

1. Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (a cross-checking script over three or four independent readings of every code, live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.
2. 1. The standard: Recommendation ITU-R M.1677-1 (10/2009), International Morse code, was downloaded from the ITU (query 5); the recommendation's page gave "Status : In force (Main)" on 2026-10-04, so it is still the current version. Its text was extracted with pypdf (query 6). Annex 1, Part I, 1.1 defines the written characters: the letters a–z and "accented e" (1.1.1), the figures 1–0 (1.1.2) and, in 1.1.3, 13 punctuation marks and signs with a written sign (full stop, comma, colon, question mark, apostrophe, hyphen, fraction bar, left and right bracket, inverted commas, double hyphen, cross and commercial at), the multiplication sign × (the same signal as the letter X, which 3.2.1 says to send for it) and six procedural signals without a written sign (understood, error, invitation to transmit, wait, end of work, starting signal). The recommendation is © ITU, all rights reserved, so it is used for verification only: the deck takes no text from it.
3. 2. Wikidata (content): every statement of P3295 (code) whose value consists of dots and dashes was fetched with query 1; those with the qualifier P3294 (encoding) Morse code (Q79897) cover all 26 letters, the 10 digits, É, 12 of the 13 ITU punctuation marks (the full stop item Q172008 has no code statement), and a number of non-ITU characters (Ä, Ö, À, Ü, &, !, ;, $, _ and others). The items of the cards, and of SOS (Q214266), distress signal (Q2355426) and prosign for Morse code (Q7250609), were then fetched in full with wbgetentities (query 2, fetch_entities.py), keeping the raw responses (entities.json): the code statements with their qualifiers and ranks, and the English, Swedish and multilingual (mul) labels and aliases. SOS has no code statement; its English aliases include the code "· · · – – – · · ·". A later query (query 15) listed every item that shares the code of the cards with back notes: the × item (Q1900125, en label "×", sv label "multiplikationstecken") has −··− and the en dash item (Q13219273, en label "–", sv label "vanligt tankstreck") has −····−, both with encoding Morse code; no item for a division sign, a subtraction or minus sign or a fraction bar has a code, so the notes do not name them.
4. 3. Pub. 102 (content): the US edition of the International Code of Signals, 1969 edition revised 2003, prepared and published by the National Imagery and Mapping Agency, a work of the US Government with no copyright claimed. The official current download from NGA and the US Coast Guard's copy answered 403 to the research environment (query 7), so the scan on archive.org was used (query 8): the archive.org OCR text cannot read the dots and dashes, so the pages were rendered as images with pypdfium2 (render.py, query 9) and read by eye. Page 17 (Chapter 1, Section 10, Morse symbols) gives the code of the 26 letters, the 10 numerals and the procedure signals AR, AS and AAA; page 20 gives their meanings (AAA "Full stop or decimal point", AR "Ending signal or End of Transmission or signal", K "Invitation to transmit"); page 139 (Chapter 4, Section 1, Distress signals, from the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea 1972) gives SOS as the group • • • – – – • • •. The page-17 table and the SOS group were transcribed by hand into verify.py (query 12).
5. 4. 33 CFR 87.01 (content): the US Inland Navigation Rules' Annex IV, distress signals, was fetched from the eCFR versioner API (query 10; the renderer address and the date-less request failed, see the queries): paragraph (d) gives SOS as ". . . - - - . . .".
6. 5. English Wikipedia (verification): the article "Morse code" and the article "SOS" were fetched as wikitext with their revision ids (query 11, fetch_wiki.py). The table under Characters and prosigns gives each character's code as a {{morse|dot|dash…}} template; the article states that É is the only accented character of the ITU standard and lists Å, Ä, Ö and others under diacritics and non-Latin extensions.
7. 6. Cross-check (verify.py, query 12): the script parses four independent readings of each card's code — the ITU text (letters and figures by tokens, punctuation by the line ending "[sign] code"), the hand transcription of Pub. 102, the Wikidata code statements with encoding Morse code (non-deprecated), and the English Wikipedia table — converts every notation (". −" in the ITU text, "• –" in Pub. 102, ".-" in Wikidata, "· · · – – –" in the SOS alias, dot/dash in the Wikipedia templates) to the deck's notation and fails on any disagreement. It also checks that no two cards share a code (which bidirectional study requires), that no two fronts are the same, that every code uses only the two signs of the notation, and that every ITU character with a written sign has a card except ×. All 51 cards agree in every source that has them: ITU, Pub. 102, Wikidata and Wikipedia for the 36 letters and digits; ITU, Wikidata and Wikipedia for É and 12 punctuation marks; ITU, Pub. 102 (AAA) and Wikipedia for the full stop; Pub. 102, 33 CFR 87.01, Wikidata (alias) and Wikipedia for SOS. The script wrote its readings to readings.json, and the evidence of every card was generated from them by make_dossier.py (query 13), not typed by hand. The scripts are not published with the deck; the rules above are what they do.
8. 7. Notation: the deck writes a dot as · (U+00B7 MIDDLE DOT) and a dash as − (U+2212 MINUS SIGN), with no spaces between the elements of a character. This keeps the code of the full stop (·−·−·−) and of the hyphen (−····−) distinct from the characters themselves, which the ASCII notation ".-" would not. The ITU prints the dot as a full stop and the dash as a minus sign with spaces between them, Pub. 102 as • and –; the elements are the same.
9. 8. Swedish text: the cards' codes and characters have no language (zxx). The front notes of the 13 punctuation cards name the mark in English and Swedish: the English and Swedish Wikidata labels where the item has them (full stop/punkt, comma/kommatecken, colon/kolon, question mark/frågetecken, apostrophe/apostrof, hyphen/bindestreck, slash/snedstreck, equals sign/likhetstecken, plus sign/plustecken, at sign/snabel-a), and for the parentheses and the quotation mark, whose Unicode-character items have no Swedish label, "vänsterparentes", "högerparentes" (Swedish Wikipedia, Parentes) and "citattecken" (Swedish Wikipedia, Citattecken). The front of the SOS card reads "SOS (distress signal)" / "SOS (nödsignal)" (Swedish Wikipedia, SOS: "den internationella nödsignalen i morsekod"). The back notes are the compiler's own wording of facts stated in the content sources: × and the dash share the codes of X and the hyphen (Wikidata, with the sv labels "multiplikationstecken" and "vanligt tankstreck"), K is the invitation to transmit and the signal of + the ending signal AR (Pub. 102), and SOS is the distress signal of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, sent as one group (Pub. 102, 33 CFR 87.01). The ITU recommendation and Wikipedia only confirmed them. The Swedish name of those regulations, "de internationella sjövägsreglerna", was checked on Swedish Wikipedia (Sjövägsreglerna, query 16).
10. 9. Machine checks by the builder against live Wikidata: for every card with a code statement, that the item has P3295 with the card's code in Wikidata's notation (".-" for ·−) and that it is the right character (its English or multilingual label or alias is the character; for the punctuation marks also its English and Swedish names). The builder's checks cannot see the P3294 qualifier; that it is Morse code (Q79897) for each of these values was checked in queries 1 and 2. For SOS: that Q214266 is an instance of prosign for Morse code (Q7250609) and of distress signal (Q2355426) and has the alias "· · · – – – · · ·" (a free-text alias, the only place Wikidata gives the code of SOS); for the notes of X and the hyphen, that Q1900125 (×) and Q13219273 (en dash) have the same P3295 code. The built deck was validated with the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators (validate_sources.ts).
11. 10. Excluded after research: Å, Ä and Ö. Wikidata gives Ä ·−·− and Ö −−−· (and À ·−−·− but no code for Å), Wikipedia lists all three among the non-ITU extensions, and the Swedish Wikipedia says they were not in the original alphabet and "senare har fått sina speciella kombinationer"; the same article also says that the code of Å was created at the International Telegraph Conference in Paris in 1865 ("Det var där koden för vårt svenska Å föddes"), the ITU's founding conference. None of them is in the current recommendation, ITU-R M.1677-1, and no current ITU or official Swedish source defining them was found (a web search, query 14, found only amateur and private pages), so they are left out (see Selection).

## Selection

Every written character except × of the International Morse code in Recommendation ITU-R M.1677-1, Annex 1, Part I, 1.1, the standard in force on 4 October 2026: the 26 letters A–Z, the accented letter É (the only one the ITU defines), the 10 digits 0–9 and the 13 punctuation marks and signs . , : ? ' - / ( ) " = + @; and the distress signal SOS, which is not in the ITU recommendation but is the Morse distress signal of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (Pub. 102) and of the US Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 87.01). 51 cards. Letters are shown in upper case (the code has no case). Left out: the multiplication sign ×, which the ITU sends with the signal of the letter X (named in the note of X instead); the six procedural signals without a written sign (understood, error, invitation to transmit, wait, end of work and the starting signal), because the deck asks for a character's code and "invitation to transmit" is the letter K (named in K's note); characters not in the current ITU recommendation, such as the national extensions Å, Ä, Ö, Ü, À and Ñ (Å's code dates from the Paris telegraph conference of 1865, but it is not in ITU-R M.1677-1 and no current official source defines Å, Ä and Ö for Swedish) and some of which share a code with each other (À and Å), and non-ITU punctuation such as ! & ; $ _ ; American Morse and other historical codes; and Q codes and abbreviations such as CQ.

## Queries

**1. Every P3295 (code) statement whose value consists of dots and dashes, with its encoding qualifier, rank and labels (sh <scratch>/run.sh q1, which runs: curl -s -H "User-Agent: solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" -H "Accept: text/csv" --data-urlencode "query@<scratch>/q1.rq" https://query.wikidata.org/sparql -o <scratch>/q1.csv). Found by first searching for literal codes (curl -s -G -A "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)" -H "Accept: text/csv" --data-urlencode 'query=SELECT ?s ?p ?o WHERE { VALUES ?o { "...---..." ".-" "·−" "· −" "▄ ▄▄▄" "-----" "−−−−−" "...−−−..." "···−−−···" } ?s ?p ?o } LIMIT 100' https://query.wikidata.org/sparql), which found P3295 on Q9659 (A) and Q204 (0); a property search for "Morse code" and "Morse" (wbsearchentities, type=property) found none, and P3020, suggested by the brief, is "residence time of water".** (Wikidata: the Morse code (P3295 code, with P3294 encoding Q79897) of each character's item, and the item SOS (Q214266))

```
SELECT ?item ?en ?sv ?code ?encoding ?encodingLabel ?rank WHERE {
  ?item p:P3295 ?st .
  ?st ps:P3295 ?code ; wikibase:rank ?rank .
  OPTIONAL { ?st pq:P3294 ?encoding . ?encoding rdfs:label ?encodingLabel FILTER(LANG(?encodingLabel) = "en") }
  FILTER(REGEX(?code, "^[-.·−–— ]+$"))
  OPTIONAL { ?item rdfs:label ?en FILTER(LANG(?en) = "en") }
  OPTIONAL { ?item rdfs:label ?sv FILTER(LANG(?sv) = "sv") }
}
ORDER BY ?code

```

## Quality control

6 rounds, 25 findings: 22 fixed, 0 rejected after checking, 3 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (131 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Machine checks and sources: every code read from three or four independent sources (ITU, Pub. 102, Wikidata, English Wikipedia; 33 CFR 87.01 for SOS) and compared by verify.py; uniqueness of every code and front; that every written ITU character has a card; licences of every source; the Wikidata checks against live Wikidata. (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 51 cards, the sources and the deck metadata.

All 51 cards agree in every source that has them, no two codes or fronts are the same, and every written ITU character except × has a card. No Wikidata check was skipped and no source disagrees with another. Findings concern the scope of the sources and two parsing slips in the script, none a card.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| (deck) | The first run of verify.py reported the digits 3 and 5 as missing from the ITU table: the running head of page 5 ("Rec. ITU-R M.1677-1 3") and the page marker "===== page 5 =====" were read as the figures 3 and 5 with an empty code. The punctuation rows of the Wikipedia table were not found either, because the article pads the sign in brackets with narrow no-break spaces (U+202F). | The letters-and-figures part of the ITU text now ends at the page break, and the Wikipedia pattern accepts U+202F. On the second run every source gave a code for every card it covers, and all agree. | fixed |
| letter-x | The ITU lists the multiplication sign × with the signal − . . −, the code of the letter X, and 3.2.1 says to send X for it. Wikidata also gives −··− on the × item (Q1900125). A card for × would have the same back as X, and the deck is studied in both directions. | No card for ×; the note of X says it is also sent for the multiplication sign. | fixed |
| letter-k | The ITU's "invitation to transmit" (− . −) is the letter K. | No separate card; K's note names the signal (ITU 1.1.3 and Part II; Pub. 102 p. 20). | fixed |
| sos | The brief names SOS as a signal from the ITU recommendation, but ITU-R M.1677-1 does not define SOS. Its content sources are the distress signals of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea as printed in Pub. 102 (p. 139) and 33 CFR 87.01 (d); Wikidata's SOS item has no code statement, only the English alias "· · · – – – · · ·", and no English or Swedish label (its label is mul "SOS"). | The card rests on Pub. 102, 33 CFR 87.01 and the Wikidata alias, checked against the English and Swedish Wikipedia; the description and selection say that SOS is not in the ITU recommendation. The Wikidata checks use the alias and the mul label. | fixed |
| full-stop | The Wikidata item for the full stop (Q172008) has no code statement, so Wikidata cannot be a content source for this card's code. | The code rests on Pub. 102 (AAA, "Full stop or decimal point", pp. 17 and 20) as the content source, checked against the ITU and Wikipedia; the Wikidata checks confirm only the item's English alias "." and its English and Swedish names used in the front note. | no change needed |
| quotation-marks | The ITU's signal is for "inverted commas (quotation marks)" [“ ”], sent before and after the quoted words; Wikidata has the same code on the items for " (U+0022), “ and ” and the fullwidth ＂. The apostrophe is printed ’ in the ITU text. | The cards show the keyboard characters " and ' with their names in the front note; the note of the quotation-marks card says the signal is sent before and after the quoted words (note later removed, round 3, first finding: it rested only on the ITU). The checks use the items for U+0022 and for the apostrophe, which has both ' and ’ as aliases. | no change needed |
| (deck) | Å, Ä and Ö, asked for by the brief if defined: they are not in ITU-R M.1677-1 (whose only accented letter is É), and no official Swedish definition was found. Wikidata has codes for Ä and Ö but not Å, and gives À the code that Swedish sources use for Å; Wikipedia lists them as non-ITU extensions. | Left out; the description and the selection say so. | fixed |
| (deck) | Every front except SOS is a character with no language (zxx), but the sides must name the deck's languages: with both sides ["zxx"] the deck would have no dcterms:language, as the roman-numerals dossier found. | The front side is declared ["en", "sv"], the languages of the SOS front and of the front notes; the builder accepts the zxx fronts as text in no language by exception. The deck's languages are English and Swedish. | no change needed |
